title: Random Numbers with <random>
html:
Modern C++ separates engines (sources of random bits) from distributions (shape the bits into the numbers you want). Forget rand() % n.

Engine + distribution

Exact numbers from a seeded engine are reproducible for a given standard library, but distributions are implementation-defined, so libc++ and libstdc++ may print different dice rolls for the same seed.

Seeding

DistributionProduces
uniform_int_distribution<int>(a, b)Integers in [a, b]
uniform_real_distribution<double>(a, b)Reals in [a, b)
normal_distribution<double>(mean, sd)Gaussian
bernoulli_distribution(p)true with probability p
discrete_distribution<int>{w...}Index i with probability ∝ wᵢ
poisson_distribution, exponential_distributionCounts, waiting times
Do

Create one engine (seeded once) and reuse it; pass it by reference to functions that need randomness.

Avoid

Re-creating std::mt19937 rng(std::random_device{}()) on every call, or rand() % 6 (biased, low quality, global state).

Watch out

std::mt19937 is fast and statistically good but not cryptographically secure — never use it for passwords, tokens or keys.

What's wrong with rand() % n?

rand() has implementation-defined (often poor) quality and a range that may be as small as 32767; % n introduces modulo bias when RAND_MAX + 1 isn't a multiple of n; and it uses hidden global state that's not thread-safe. <random> fixes all three.
